utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this day I wish to greet Mr. Praljak, the accused, ladies and gentlemen, members of the counsel, Mr. Stringer and his assistant, and everyone else assisting us. We're going to continue with the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Stringer, and I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon to Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we -- yesterday, you may see it on the screen there in front of you, I don't know if it's in your binder, we were talking about one of the articles from the Hrvatski Vojna, the Croatian Soldier magazine. That was 3D01281. You don't need to go to it because I've finished asking my questions about that. I'm going to move on to the next few documents in this binder before we conclude this part of the cross-examination. The next document, General, should be P00191, 191. Do you have that? It's a document dated the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document. I think it's the 7th of May. The one I have, the date is the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm sorry if I misspoke. It's the 7th of May, 1992. Do you recognise this document, General? This appears to be over the signature of Janko Bobetko, and it relates to the transition or the turnover of command from you to a Zdravko Andabak in the southern front. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2, General Bobetko orders that you are to inform Brigadier Andabak about the situation in the sector that you've been in charge of thus far, and then it continues in the next paragraph to say that: "The hand-over of duty will take place in my presence at 1600 hours on the 8th of May, 1992, in accordance with the law on armed forces of the Republic of Croatia." And then it says: "General Praljak will submit a complete report on the situation and problems in the sector." General, simply the question here is: This procedure that is set out on the transfer of the command from you to Brigadier Andabak, would it have been customary or expected that upon handing over the command to your successor you would brief him on the situation in the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, I did so. Actually, I found the person who would replace me. I asked him to be kind enough to come. He resisted to some extent because he said that he wasn't educated enough to head the sector as -- though he was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or at least he originates from there, but I didn't do that in Grude, and I never saw this document before studying the documentation that was here in the Tribunal. I had to go back to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you nonetheless provide Brigadier Andabak with a full briefing about the situation in your area of responsibility before you turned the command over to him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I knew I conveyed to him to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's really essential that you do that, isn't it, so that when he takes command he immediately has to have a good grasp, a very good grasp, of all of the information on the ground so that he can command effectively; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so. One needs to have control of all the available information at that point in time. Though there wasn't anything in particular, things were very simple basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm going to move forward now to the 8th or the 9th of November, 1993, to the time when you again handed over command to a successor, and on the 9th of November, 1993, you handed over command of the HVO Main Staff to Ante Roso. And I take it, General, that the situation was a good deal more complex at that time than perhaps it was back in May of 1992 when you handed over command to Brigadier Andabak. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation in May 1992 was extremely complex in view of the fact that the Army of Republika Srpska, or they were still mostly the JNA -- actually, on the 10th of April when they captured Kupres with a tank brigade and after that attacked Livno, they were moving towards Split, Makarska Ploce as part of their broader strategic plan, and the situation for Bosnia and Herzegovina was extremely, extremely difficult. And for Croatia, of course, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the 6th of May of this year, which is a couple of days after you began giving your evidence, this is what you told us about the hand-over from you to General Roso in November of 1993 -- Judge Antonetti was asking you a question, and I think he was looking at the document that's the next document in your binder, which is P06556. And Judge Antonetti asked you, this is page 39665 of the transcript,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI SAID
utterances.text: "As far as you remember, are you sure that you told him everything? Did you remember that you told him everything, that you drew him the full picture of what was happening, giving him details as to the positions of the HVO on the field," et cetera? So -- and Judge Antonetti then says: "When you handed over your duties did you do it according to the state of the ART?" And your response was: "Your Honour, all the data, all the facts, I precisely gave to General Roso, and that wasn't difficult to do because he had been a member of the HVO before. He was a commander of Livno." I'm skipping a sentence, and you say: "He was a man who knew the situation relatively well. He wasn't far from the events." So again, General, just as to this particular turnover from you to General Roso, then, I take it that you'd agree that it was extremely important that at the time he assumed command of the HVO on the 9th of November, 1993, it was imperative that General Roso had a full and complete picture of the situation on the ground within his entire area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking would you agree with me that it was imperative that he had a good grasp of the situation within his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know how to measure the importance in degrees. There's a certain number of military information, maps, and so on that the new commander has to be briefed on. Furthermore, there's the staff waiting for him, and he has to be familiarised with the most important things. It's not possible to go into minor details, hundreds of minor details. All the most important information are conveyed. Let me not list them all. The position, the strength, the previous battles, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And moving ahead, the next exhibit is P02902, and this is, I believe, one of the Spanish Battalion reports that we looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because it's an UNPROFOR report, Mr. President, I think we can't show it on the monitors outside the courtroom, although it is -- we can talk about it. And, General, I showed this to you before. I don't think this is controversial or in dispute. On page 4 of the English version, General, in yours there's a section of the Spanish Battalion report relating to Jablanica-Konjic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there are about four -- three or four paragraphs there and then there's one sentence with the number 1 in front of it, and it says: "Fierce fighting in the area of Boksevica is continuing. HVO troops are under the command of General Praljak and Colonel Miro Andric." So I think I asked you this before, General. During this period of time, which is the 22nd of June, 1993, you were, in fact, present in the Jablanica area around Boksevica, and you were engaged in activities as a commander of HVO forces, true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. I was not near Jablanica. I was not near Boksevica. I was at Boksevica for a certain fixed number of days. We were protecting a small part of that mountain, the last part that we still had control over for the civilian population and part of the HVO forces to be able to pull out, which we finally succeeded in doing. Only that and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you were at Boksevica on or about the 22nd of June, 1993. And if you look at the next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It says here that I was. Their information are frequently vague --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, General. Maybe we're --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the HVO has the most modern weapons, mostly American, that simply is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. I'm not asking if you agree with the report. You've given me the answer I was looking for. You said: "I was at Boksevica for a certain fixed number of days." Now, is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, but not on the 22nd, a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tell us the dates.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we withdrew on the 8th or 9th of July, and I was there for about 12 days, I think, roughly. Plus, minus a day or two. It's simply difficult to say. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to skip over one document and I'm going to move to P03516, 3516. And this is from the 17th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, before you continue, I should like to return to the first document for an additional question which I consider to be important. It is P191. General Praljak, you have the document in your language in front of you. As I read this document, General Bobetko, who is in command of the southern front of Croatia in the month of May 1992, the date being important, he's at Ploce, which is an enchanting port not far from Dubrovnik, and that is where the forward command post was situated. And he decided, following a suggestion and a request from Susak, to carry out a change and to appoint Andabak in your place to become commander of the Mostar-Siroki Brijeg-Citluk-Capljina sector. The month of May, and this is important as the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is already a state, and a state other than Croatia appoints a commander, Andabak, in your place in a sector which juridically does not belong to the Republic of Croatia. And looking at this document, I said to myself that a reasonable Judge could draw the conclusion from this that this document is proof of the involvement of the Republic of Croatia in the development of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina since Andabak is taking your place in territory which, according to international law, is under the competence or authority of a legitimate government, that of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is one approach. However, thinking things over, I wondered whether there might be a second approach which I would like to elaborate on. We are in the month of May. There's the aggression of the Serbs against Croatia, and the Republic of Croatia is endeavouring as best it can to protect itself and decides within the framework of a plan of defence to appoint commanders who will be responsible for certain geographical areas, and in the contemporary world we see this certain state, such as the United States, appoint generals external to the United States that have competence over certain areas without infringing upon the sovereignty of states. So how could you explain that you, who was in command before May and then Andabak takes your place, whereas there is a sovereign state there. Would you support the first hypothesis or the second one? I hope you understood, because my question was rather lengthy, but the issue is rather complicated and I need to elaborate for you to be able to answer, because this document is a document involving the implication of the Republic of Croatia if one reads it as it stands, but there may be another explanation, and that's what I'm waiting for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, your first thesis is correct legally speaking. If there's no war and when the central authority is functioning and when the central authority has prepared for war and when the aggressor comes from the outside, all that you said in your hypothesis stands. However, the central authority in Sarajevo is surrounded and is unable to communicate with anyone. Furthermore, the central authority had not prepared in any way, nor does it have any representative throughout this area from Livno, Kupres, Bugojno, who could in any way and with any means organise anything. We just have the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska. Then the people rose up in our -- on their own accord. Everyone starts digging in around their own municipalities, finding whatever ways they can. First of all there's the treachery of the commander of Mostar who issues the order for Mostar to be abandoned. Then someone else who was acting, Mikulic, who was acting HVO commander, was simply uncapable of doing that job. And I was there towards the end of March, and having returned to Zagreb I asked, I requested from Minister Susak and President Tudjman that this should take place, what we see in this document, otherwise, this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be totally occupied and a part of Croatia south of Split would be in jeopardy, because if with a tank brigade they defeated the HVO in Kupres and then with a tank brigade they attacked Livno, which was under the command of Ante Gotovina at the time, and they were attacking Stolac which they had captured, you know everything about Mostar, and unless Croatia extends certain assistance in terms of personnel and organisation, it's all over. And that was when General Bobetko, who had a position in the training in the Main Staff, was appointed, and he took over to assist in organising the Main Staff of the HVO, which was taken over by General Petkovic, and he helped him and issued him orders until the HVO reached a level when it could take over and act independently. Of course I went there on my own initiative in a certain sense and took over control of this zone, and when I stabilised the situation, I had to return to Zagreb where I was employed. But I kept coming back there and running those operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand you well, you're telling us that due to the fact that the central government in Sarajevo could not confront the situation, the Republic of Croatia felt that it was necessary, in view of the Serb offensive, to assist this territory because there was danger for the Republic of Croatia. Is that how one should understand it? And to complete the picture, let us imagine that there's an enemy, X, that is attacking the United States, and in Canada there's no government, and at that point in time the United States would appoint a general, any general, in Montreal to take over the area in view of the fact that there was no government left there. Is that how one could describe it? Is my example a good one with Canada and the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. Because otherwise they would attack America as well. Dubrovnik was totally surrounded, the south of Croatia cut off. So if they let them move towards Split, the fact that a country has been recognised is very important but insignificant. Cyprus has been recognised and it is divided for the past 50 years. Certain things are recognised but in military terms you can try to establish justice and seek justice 50 years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the document that I was just taking you to is P03516. 3516, which is -- do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a report of Colonel Siljeg dated 17th of July, 1993. Now, there's a lot of information in here, but really the only piece of information that I'm interested in at this point is on page 5 of the English, which is toward the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm awfully sorry, Mr. Stringer. I should perhaps not do this, but I think it's my duty to try to have clarity, and the witness has brought Cyprus into the play. It's on page 11, line 5, and for the life of me I do not understand what connection there is. Could you -- could you explain what you meant? Or maybe it was a misunderstanding and you didn't speak of Cyprus at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did speak about Cyprus, yes. There was no misunderstanding there at all. Despite the fact that Cyprus was an integral state when it was recognised by the United Nations and the European Union, it is still divided in military terms. And the same thing could have happened to Croatia. For example, the Army of Republika Srpska and the JNA could have taken the southern part of Croatia. Croatia would have still remained a recognised independent state, but still it would have lost its southern part, and then we would go on seeking justice for 50 years all over the world in order to connect the two parts of our state. We didn't not have any guarantees despite the fact, Judge Trechsel, that we were recognised. Nobody offered us any guarantees. Nobody told us, You are now recognised, our borders will be protected, no aggression will be allowed from now on. Everything remained as it was until 1995 until there was a military operation to liberate the occupied parts of Croatia. I would have been so much happier if things could have been resolved in a different way, but they could not have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to prolong the debate about Cyprus, but I have to say that very clearly it has -- the Cyprus case has nothing to do with Croatia and what happened in the 1990s there. Cyprus was recognised by actually almost by all the states concerned. By the way, the UN, the United Nations, has never recognised any state. It only admits a state, but it is not the recognition itself. Let us make it clear, number one. Number two, Cyprus has been divided only at a later stage, not at the -- at the inception of the independence but later on when -- when due to some other events which I do not want to go into, when Turkey -- the Turkish state has helped the secession of the Turks living in Cyprus there. So it is another issue, and I believe that this comparison is really far-fetched, but of course you have the right to bring any example of what you think fits, but I just wanted to tell you about this and the Court as far as Cyprus is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. I think you did not actually draw a direct parallel, but what you made was a hypothetical remark extrapolating what historical developments might have happened if you had not intervened, if Croatia had not intervened. That is how I understand you now, and it seems that you agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. My parallel concerned the following: Cyprus was also a state and there was an aggression, and nobody provided us with any guarantees that the JNA would not remain in the occupied territories for 40 years onwards. Nobody gave us any such guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have clarified the point. Excuse me, please, Mr. Stringer. I'm not very happy about having interrupted you so brutally. I hope you do not feel now divided like Cyprus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it didn't feel brutal. Occupied is perhaps a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P03516, General, is the document we were looking at, and I'd like to take you to paragraph 10 which is towards the end of the document in this report of Colonel Siljeg where he's saying "Brada" or "Beardie" visited this area for longer and he is acquainted with the situation in detail, and, "We all know the situation very well. Perhaps some individuals bury their heads in the sand and do not want to know in order to avoid responsibility, yet they do not know that ignorance does not free them from responsibility." Now, we're going to talk about this document in greater detail when we talk about Prozor, General, but the point for our purposes here is that of the 17th of July, the fact is that even though you weren't the commander of the HVO Main Staff at that time, you had a very solid grasp and familiarity with the situation as it existed throughout the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone of the HVO; isn't that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. I was familiar with the situation, because I had been there before. I was around Prozor, Vakuf, and I was in Central Bosnia for two months -- or, rather, a month and a half, to be more precise. On the 17th I had already left when he issued this report. So one could say that I had a relatively good knowledge of the military situation, the intentions of the Army of Republika Srpska, and the developments which concerned the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes. Not in great -- very great detail, but I was familiar with the gist of the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. I seem to understand that Beardie is a nickname for the general, and I think it's good to have it said for the transcript. I was first wondering what this referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, can we agree that the reference to Brada or Beardie in this report is a reference to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report probably, or very likely this is me, but I was not the only one who bore that nickname. There were some other people who sported beards and are referred to as Brada, but in this particular document I would be almost sure that this nickname refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, General, I want to talk for a minute or two, then, about the transition from General Petkovic to you on or about the 24th of July, 1993, because I haven't seen any documents on an official form of transfer such as the ones we've seen in the last few minutes. At the time that -- actually, I know that there is one. I know that there is one from Mate Boban, but I want to ask you specifically. Did you receive a formal briefing from General Petkovic on the 24th or at about the 24th of July as you assumed formal command of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for a formal briefing, because General Petkovic remained in the area constantly, unlike me who left. He was my deputy, my second in command. Of course we talked about everything, but there was no need for too many words to be said between the two of us, because I was familiar with most of the things. Until that moment we had known each other well. We were familiar with all the military problems, of course. And given the fact that Bugojno had already -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intervention for the transcript, just for the clarity of the transcript. The general didn't say that there was a formal briefing but a formal takeover.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no formal takeover.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a formal briefing but not a formal takeover.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a formal takeover in term of signing the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the questions are put by Mr. Stringer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I was going to -- let me clarify, because maybe -- I don't know if there was an interpretation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There was a document in which the command was formally transferred to you from General Petkovic; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Mate Boban appointed me as commander, and General Petkovic informed the units and the operation zones that as of that date the commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council was Slobodan Praljak. We did not sign any formal documents, because General Petkovic remained there in the area. And second of all, there was not too much time to spend talking because Bugojno had already fallen, and we had to start salvaging what could be salvaged given the military situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. So my question was about whether there was a formal briefing that you received from General Petkovic, and if I understood you correctly, you said no; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "formal briefing"? What is your idea of a formal briefing? When you say "formal," do you mean sitting at a table? Yes, if you mean that, yeah. People sit down. The newly appointed general comes and talks to his deputy. If you think that that is formal, then, yes, there was some form, but there was no line-up of the troops because there was no need or time to do that. So in that sense there was no formality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you seem to be surprised by the questions that Mr. Stringer is putting to you, or even by the questions that the Judges, like myself, for example, put to you. Prior to the 24th of July, Mr. Petkovic was the HVO commander. Mr. Petkovic - and this is something we've seen in other documents - also participated in meetings with the international community and with Halilovic, meetings that had to do with the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. The media that covered this perhaps weren't fully aware of who was in command of what. The documents that we have from the Spanish Battalion and so on, well, show that they were often not aware of the roles various people played, but on the 24th of July you assumed this post, and at that point in time it was quite natural that people should be aware of the fact that you were then the military commander, and the international community was aware of the fact that the HVO had a new individual at its head, in this particular case, Slobodan Praljak. And when this assumption of power took place, it was necessary for there to be documents. Words don't seem to be sufficient. Mr. Stringer says I've such documents, I haven't seen any. There are others, though, for Andabak who succeeded you. So that's the situation. We are trying to understand how this was done because there's something else at stake behind all of this, and as you as a cultivated and intelligent individual, you are surely aware of the fact in the theory presented by the Prosecution, you could have had de facto command. So prior to the 24th of July in reality it was perhaps you who were at the head, the number-one person, and Petkovic was perhaps just a puppet. And on the 24th of July, the puppet was officially replaced by yourself. So that could be an explanation. That could explain the fact that there are no documents. So the questions aren't as innocent as you may think, because what is at stake is the issue of de facto command. So do try to enlighten us, to help us understand why there was no official takeover, because as you know, and you know better than anyone else, as a commander one exercises the supreme authority. One exercises supreme authority. So if Petkovic gave over power to you, according to 7(1), Article 7(1), you are at that point in time the most responsible individual. He is no longer the most responsible individual. So everyone and Mr. Stringer are putting questions to you. The Judges would also like to know why there was no official takeover supported by documents showing that there was a takeover. Do you now understand better why these questions are being put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Yes, I do. You know, Your Honours, over there in that area, theatre plays were being played. The Spanish Battalion had its own theatre play. UNPROFOR had one as well. Everybody wrote scenarios, sent reports. There were meetings being held, negotiations, talks, Geneva talks and others, and within all that everybody printed a lot of material. Some were engaged in smuggling. There was all sorts of things. The fact remains, however, that the BiH army was attacking all that time, and that was a fact. And General Petkovic and some other commanders were being summoned to meetings to sign cease-fire accords. Everybody was trying to trick everybody else and trying not to portray things the way they were. They were blind. They didn't see the problem. They were playing games, offering empty words about the causes and reasons for a war since the situation was very difficult and dramatic. I was a friend of Petkovic's. I was his colleague. We had never had any prior conflicts or discords. So our takeover took half an hour. We did not even use big words. I just used his name. I told him, Pele, I'm off to Vakuf because after the fall of Bugojno everything is over. You stay here, see about Central Bosnia. We will ask for Tole to come down here because we cannot manage things from one place anymore. So I did not use any theatricals, although I am a theatre director. I did not do like UNPROFOR. I did not have the time or need to inform anybody, to announce my arrival, to go for a meeting to the Spanish Battalion where I would be formally received, given lunch, wined and dined. Your Honours, we were under a heavy aggression. Later on at one point when the situation calmed down somewhat, I did hold a meeting in Tomislavgrad to which I summoned all representatives of the international community, and then at that meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'll stop you there. We should understand your answer to mean that the situation was such that you needed no more than ten minutes for the takeover with General Petkovic, and then each one of you continued with their duties. You were in Gornji Batkovic [as interpreted], Petkovic and Tole were elsewhere. That's what you have said. Everyone understands you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for your use of the word "puppet." Could you imagine a situation where a two-star general who spent 12 days at Boksevica leading a group of 50 men to preserve an area and received orders from General Petkovic, and then you say that Petkovic was a puppet and I was his commander. No. Until that moment, it was my decision to go to Boksevica to put myself at everybody's disposal because of the situation that was critical. And I had brought my men after I spent several -- a lot of time in Kostajnica. I took arms in my hands. I stayed there as a foot soldier until we stopped the aggression. On the last day before we pulled from Boksevica, Petkovic did appoint me commander but it was already too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P04699. We've seen this before. It's part of a larger report related to the Defence Department of the HVO, and if you would turn to page 25 of your version, page 16 of the English. I'm just going to use this to ask you about your knowledge of one situation as of the time that you took command of the HVO Main Staff. The fourth paragraph of the English on page 16 it says -- and this report relates to the period of January to June 1993. It says: "In the period, over six thousand prisoners of war stayed in appropriate centres on the territory of the H-B. There are currently over four thousand captives."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Can you repeat the page number? I can't find it on page 25 of the Croatian text. Would you please give me the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've got it as page 25 for you. I don't have the ERN number for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, on page 25 I can't see anything about that. I really done know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll set the document aside and I'll just ask a question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. Yes. The second paragraph. I apologise. I didn't see it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thanks to counsel for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I think it would be helpful if you told us whose report this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a -- I thought I did, Your Honour. It's a report of the Defence Department. It relates to activities of various parts of the Defence Department during January to June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, it's making reference to large numbers, thousands of persons who were being held as captives or prisoners in the HZ HB as of the time of this report, which was adopted on the 7th of August, 1993. Now, it says that: "There are currently over four thousand captives. Several hundred of them are members of the Serbian Army while a huge number are members of the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." General, I just wanted to use this to ask you the question: At the time you took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, 1993, you were aware that hundreds or thousands of Muslim individuals were being detained in HVO facilities in Herceg-Bosna? You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. After Boksevica, after I left from Bosnia and Herzegovina and returned, you know how things were day in and day out. I didn't have the time or any information with regard of what is stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you're aware that beginning in the days following the 30th of June, 1993, that an order went out to arrest and detain all the Muslim men of military age throughout the areas of the South-East and North-West Herzegovina Operative Zones. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you at the time that you were present down in Herceg-Bosna during July and August of 1993, weren't you aware that that's what was taking place? All the Muslim military-aged men were being arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. From the 24th until -- well, I spent a lot of that time, and I did things according to a procedure that I described for you. You can see what I did every single day, and you know very well what information I had available to me. I did not have either the time or information as to who was where. Very well. Go on then. Ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a yes or no answer, I think. Weren't you aware --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were not aware?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was aware of the existence of the prisons. I was aware of their existence. I even sent offenders there, as you could see from some documents, and that's the end of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, were you aware of an order to remove Muslims who had been members of the HVO and to disarm them after the attack occurred on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at the time you took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, 1993, General Petkovic didn't tell you about any of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not have any time to talk about that. Bugojno fell and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I'm going to challenge you on that. You've been sitting in this courtroom for a long time. You know that on the day you took command of the HVO Main Staff, you and your HVO had thousands of Muslim men who were being held prisoner in various HVO detention facilities. Isn't that true? You know now at the very least that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me what I knew at the time, and I'm telling you that I did not know that. If you're asking me when I learnt about the existence of prisons with a certain number of prisoners there, then I can tell you that this was after a text was published in Globus, when I spoke to three journalists. And we have always spoken about that. On the 1st of September I gave them --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you learnt about all these prisoners from a journalist. You did not learn about any of these prisoners from General Petkovic at the time he turned the command over to you. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear anything about that, and I really don't know what would have General Petkovic had to do with prisons. Prisons had nothing whatsoever to do with the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Even if members of the various operative zones were involved in arresting and detaining all these people? You're saying the HVO armed forces has no responsibility for them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question. When you say different commanders of different operative zones, that doesn't mean anything to me. You have to specify who, at what time. And while I was in command, if anybody participated in what you're referring to, then I could answer whether I knew of those things, what I knew, how I reacted. When you say different people participated in different things is too vague for me to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated there was no type to talk about prisoners at the time you assumed command of the HVO. You mentioned Bugojno. So is it true, General, that events on the ground, military operations, were the only thing that concerned you, and the fact that you had all these prisoners on your hands at the time you took command was not something that you ever concerned yourself with when you were acting as commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did I not have the time, but also no conversation about takeover has to concern itself with prisons, because this is not within the purview of the Main Staff. I really don't know how to answer your question, because you're implying that prisoners were under the authority of the Main Staff, which is incorrect. So my answer is yes, up to the 1st of September, until I was called by Mrs. -- I really can't remember. Oh, yes. Her name was Mrs. Ivanisevic, and she told me that there was something there, and then I -- well, okay then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to come back and talk about the prisoner and the camp issues later on. Just to finish this based on what you've said -- I should follow up though. You said prisoners were not under the authority of the Main Staff. Are you telling us then that the prisoners were under the authority of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that whenever someone is captured, it was one's duty to handover the prisoners to the military police. As to who was responsible, you've heard witnesses here. It's not for me to meddle in things that I'm not well informed of. My claim is clear. The Main Staff, while I was there, had nothing to do with this, nor should it have had anything to do with this matter. That's not part of the descriptions of the duties that I was to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to this issue at a later point. General, the next exhibit is P04719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'd like to ask you something about the document. There's a takeover of power, and you tell us that General Petkovic didn't tell you that there were prisoners, and so on and so forth. Very well. Why not? But you will admit that it might seem surprising for someone looking at this from the outside. For example, if in Baghdad a general is replaced by another general, I suppose that the American general will tell his successor, "We have such and such a number of prisoners in our prisons," and then they'll take stock of the military situation. But you say no, this issue was not raised. While listening to you, I was wondering why. Was it because of the situation, because he was fighting and at that point in time there was a rapid takeover, and you both thought that the other person was well-informed? That's perhaps true. I don't have any information that would allow me to conclude that you are not telling the truth. I just don't know. I'm trying to analyse serenely the nature of the situation. And what also might seem surprising is the fact that you say that you didn't know that the Muslims had been disarmed and imprisoned. That might also seem surprising, but it could be true because you were perhaps in an area where you weren't confronted with such problems, and as a result you weren't informed of them. So this takeover of power with Petkovic, where did it physically take place? Was it over the phone? Did it take place physically? Where? How long did it last, as far as you know? Because there could be another explanation that perhaps you don't want to provide. All those in the administration, in the military administration, know that sometimes there are takeovers that are very difficult because the person leaving isn't happy. The person being replaced isn't happy and has no contact with the person replacing him, or there's a handshake and one simply leaves after that. So that could also be an explanation. That's why it's necessary to tell us precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is a lengthy one so I'll deal with the last aspect of your question first of all. It's true that when certain positions involve honours and a nice kind of life, people fight for those positions. Ninety per cent of those who held positions in the HVO would have been happy if they could have given their positions to someone else, because what does it mean to be a commander in the HVO at that time, at a time when Bugojno fell and everything was in chaos and one saw no end to the problem? And I had over 2.000 men with whom I had to fight for 20 hours continually. It was very likely that I would lose my life, or at least once a day it was more probable that I would die than survive. So, Your Honours, we keep referring to American generals, but that's not what the situation was like. There were no shifts. There were no salaries. The units were dispersed. They were small. The people were so tired that sometimes they couldn't function psychologically and physically. You'd be someone parents -- you'd act as someone's parents, and you would be with them for 20 hours a day, you'd go from one hill to another. There were 20.000 refugees, 1.500 men. Many people were completely mad. That's the first thing. And secondly, I'm not sure that an American general would talk about the number of prisoners of war if -- this is a matter for another part of the army. In Guantanamo Bay there are prisoners there, but the American General Staff wasn't in charge of them, the CIA was; so they won't be informed of the fact. So it's a matter of the organisation that has to deal with such matters. That was the case in Mostar up there. I don't know what else I can say. And this went on for 85 or -- to 90 days without a break. The conversation I had with Petkovic took place in Grude. We spoke to each other for half an hour, 45 minutes at the most. If there's anyone else, we would both have preferred to go to Makarska for a swim in the sea. The greatest problem was to convince someone to perform such duties there because everyone would say, "Well, I'm not capable of doing this. Give this position to someone else and so on." The people who remained there, the men who remained there did want to fight, but performing those duties was difficult for anyone because you saw in Siljeg's report that was shown a while ago, we didn't analyse it, though, you saw in that report that he had terrible problems he didn't know how to solve. You know, he said they were burying their heads in the sand, men were burying their heads in the sand, some had fled, so you can't compare the situation to the situation in a normal state in a normal army. There's no comparison to be made unfortunately. I would have been happy if I had had such an office, if I had my staff, if I'd just issued orders for planes to overfly an area, and so on and so forth. Unfortunately, that was not the situation, and we can't transform the situation into the situation we would have liked to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I hear again and again you are going statements which, in my view, are not very much to the point here what we are trying to achieve, so please kindly take the floor only when you are asking -- you are asked a question. And therefore now I would like to ask Mr. Stringer to continue with his questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Judge Prandler is right. You provided explanations and then you went off on a tangent, but to summarise what you have just said, I don't want to make any mistakes because all of this is very important, you met Petkovic in Grude. According to what you have said, as far as you can remember, you spoke to each other for 30 to 45 minutes. The situation in military terms was extremely complicated, and you did not raise the issue of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Citluk, Citluk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well it was in Citluk. You said Grude, you're correcting yourself. It was in Citluk. Fine. Thank you for that. General Petkovic didn't speak to you about prisoners, because these prisoners weren't the responsibility of the HVO Main Staff, and as a result it was not necessary to refer to this matter. Have I correctly summarised the reasons for which this takeover was a rapid one and the issue of prisoners was not one that was raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Try and be as concise as I have just been and we will save a lot of time. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to be most specific on this, although again we're going to come back and spend a certain amount of time on the camps, on the 24th of July, 1993, you're telling us that you did not know that the HVO was holding prisoners at its military remand prison at the Heliodrom south of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the Heliodrom was a prison, but as to who was imprisoned there, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Same question for the military remand prison at Ljubuski. Did you know that the HVO was holding hundreds of prisoners down at that facility at the time that you took command on the 24th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General Petkovic never told you about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know about Muslim prisoners being detained at the Dretelj facility in the Capljina municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of the existence –- now whether it was Dretelj or Gabela - after a telephone conversation with Ms. Ivanisevic who brought in the ZDF. I heard about the existence of something down there. Whatever I could do, well, I authorised her to enter the premises, although officially I didn't have the right to do this, but I didn't care. If that could have helped her to go there and film the situation, I gave her the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So on the 24th of July, 1993, when he turned over command of the Main Staff to you, General Petkovic didn't tell you anything about Dretelj, the Dretelj camp facility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is it also true he didn't speak to you about the Gabela prison?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, as I said, we'll come back to the camps. The next exhibit in your binder should be P04719. We're reaching the end of this section of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, without speculating, but a criminal judge likes to understand the situation in the light of various hypothesis. I'm going to formulate a hypothesis now. Let's imagine that General Petkovic said to you, "The HVO has such and such a number of prisoners." What would you have done or what would you have said, because under oath you're claiming that General Petkovic never told you anything about the matter. You've made the solemn declaration and that's what you said, so that carries a certain weight. So assuming what you say is true, well, if General Petkovic told you, "Well, we have prisoners," what would you have said, and what would you have done in such a case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. I would have continued to fight. That's the reason for which I went down there. I had no responsibility for the prisons. It was my duty to send to prison HVO members who had committed disciplinary offences. If crimes had been committed, they would be dealt with according to the procedure that you have heard about here on numerous occasions, and you've heard about the procedure from people who are more familiar with the procedure than I am. If he had said that there were prisoners, if he had told me about prisoners at the time, well, in the situation I wouldn't have done anything. I would have gone to Rama again, and I would have continued to fight. I have nothing to do with prisons. I had nothing to do with prisons. What should I have done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak at the very beginning of the trial a few years ago, time passes rapidly. You learned -- I learned at the time that you had given authorisation for prison visits. As I was previously responsible for over 50.000 prisoners and granted authorisations, I told myself if he has granted such authorisation, is he really familiar with the situation or not? If he's not familiar with the situation at that point in time, he can provide authorisation without realising what the consequences might be, and that posed a serious problem for me to see that you had provided authorisation, and then someone who writes a report, the report is then broadcast in the media, published in the media. When one hides something, well, one can't broadcast it, but the fact that you gave this authorisation, I link that -- well, I linked that at the time to the fact that you may or may not have been familiar with the situation. It's as if -- well, you're against American examples. You object to American examples. I used those examples because it's a current matter, and I try to use examples that everyone is familiar with. It's as if there was an American general who had the famous prison under his control where there were cases of abuse. He'd then give CNN authorisation to go there, interview the prisoners, the prisoners would then said, "Well, look, our heads were covered with sacks. We were beaten, and so on and so forth." And then naturally CNN would broadcast this report in such a situation, the American general who apparently gave the order -- who allegedly gave the order, well, naturally didn't know what was going on, so there we have it. Apparently General Petkovic will testify. He will be in your place. He'll make the solemn declaration, and he'll confirm or deny what you have said. So today you are telling us, "I wasn't aware of the fact that there were prisoners. I knew that there were military prisons to which certain soldiers were sent. I provided authorisation so that reports could be made," and that was without knowing whether you had the right or not to give authorisation. So this is important. Now again you are telling us you were not aware of the existence of hundreds or thousands of prisoners. And let me add something else. If you knew that there were prisoners, would you have -- if you had known there were prisoners, would you have provided these authorisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, it's specified whether there were 6.000 and so on and so forth. In there are prisons, I must have believed that there were some prisoners there, but my position was in Croatia, in my department, and while I was down there, wherever a journalist came from and whatever the journalist wanted to see, and this was not only the case for journalists but also for representatives and military attaches, for all these individuals I provided them with the authorisation to go wherever they wanted to go and to have access to all information. So when Vulliamy said, "General, will you give me authorisation?" I said go there and have a look for yourself. No one else wanted to give him authorisation. I didn't know whether to let him in or not. There was a journalist from Zagreb. I gave him the pass. They sent him back from the gate. You have his report. They said Praljak hasn't got anything to do with this here and he had to go back. The ZDF, the German television team, was allowed in. So my position was that nothing should be concealed, that there was nothing to be concealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, let me conclude. We know this is what you said, that you had high-level contact with a military attache from the US embassy in Zagreb. You would see this individual frequently, and he would take stock of the situation with you. Under oath, at no point in time did the military attache tell you, "We know through our intelligence service that you have thousands of Muslim prisoners in detention. We know that some are being abused, and this has to come to an end." He never said anything of this kind to you? Is that what you are claiming under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under oath I'm claiming that he never told me anything of this kind, nor did anyone else. You can call him. You have his statement. He could go there. He was in Rama. He could go wherever he wanted to go. From the very beginning when he arrived as a Red Cross representative to see the ports and so on and so forth, well from that point in time and onwards, he remained there until Operation Storm, during that period he had access to everything, and that wasn't only the case for this individual, there was Germans, the Spaniards, they all had access to everything. At least whenever it was possible for me to decide that they could have access, this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, we have a few more minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to challenge something you've said here in the last few minutes. The President asked you what you would have done if you had known about the prisoners, and you said, "Nothing. I would have continued to fight. That was the reason why I went down there." You said, "I had no responsibility for the prisons." Now, General, I'm going to put it to you that's an absurd assertion for you to make, because what you're saying is that even though you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, you bear no responsibility for the HVO's prisoners of war. Is that really your assertion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Prisoners of war exist, and there's no reason for them not to exist. The fact is how POWs are treated. A POW is naturally a phenomenon you encounter in all wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question. I want to try to finish off this section before the break, Mr. President. It's P04719, General. Do you recognise this as an order that you issued on or about the 1st of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what you're doing here is laying out the organisation of the command structure and offensive - defensive operations in the South-East Herzegovina operative zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. I ordered the operative zone to draft a document so that it wouldn't just be a matter of self-defence. I wanted to wake them up a bit. This order was never implemented. It never reached the operative level. However, I wanted to shake them up a bit. I didn't want them to remain on the defensive. I wanted to see whether they would be prepared to launch offensive operations as well, but this is, well, a piece of paper in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to focus on paragraph 1 and some of the units that you're asserting authority over as reflected in this order. There are references to a number of units, although most of them have abbreviations, and I just want to clarify what those abbreviations stand for. For example, you start off: "The South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone comprising 1st KD." We have in the translation KD. Is that the Knez Domagoj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then I'm going to skip to the next line. The MHC, is that the Mario Hrkac Cikota Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the next one is the KB. That's the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that is the Convicts Battalion. Isn't it, General? I think you do know. You just don't want to admit it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I knew, I'd tell you, but I don't. This list of units of such a level, well, you can see from the handwriting someone from the operative zone drafted this, and naturally you have my name here. I signed it as a document, but I don't have to be familiar with each and every unit that is referred to in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we conclude this section, I want to try and clarify the status of the Kaznjenicka Bojna, the Convicts Battalion within the HVO. I know that I asked you a couple of questions about this at the beginning, but I don't think I got it clear enough for the record. General, can we agree that the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, whatever the names were, and there were many that I didn't know, I am telling you again that at my time I had no command over Mr. Naletilic or the unit he was in command of, and I can repeat this as many times as you wish under oath. I wasn't in command of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: The question was not whether you were in command of the Convicts Battalion, but the question was that, General, and I quote, "Can we agree that the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO." Please answer to this question. Do you think that the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO or you disagree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Convicts Battalion, according to all the information I have at my disposal, was not part of the HVO, given the information I had. I wasn't in command of the unit that was under the command of Mladen Naletilic Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to need to come back to this issue perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in fact time to have a break of the we will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the hearing is resumed. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Stringer, this KB, unfortunately you give me too little time. It says here the KB Brigade, and on another page, on the second page in paragraph 2.1 it says Brigade Knez Branimir Brigade, Citluk. So it's not the convicts brigade but the Knez Branimir Brigade from Citluk. The document we're looking at now, P04719. So you asked me if it was the Convicts Battalion, it is the KB brigade, and on page 2 in paragraph 2.1, it says Knez Branimir Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I do want to bring you back to your testimony at the very end of the last session where in response to a question from Judge Prandler you said that -- this is page 37, line 17, the Convicts Battalion, according to all the information I had at my disposal, was not part of the HVO given the information I had. I wasn't in command of the unit that was under the command of Mladen Naletilic Tuta." Now, General, I just want to take a minute to talk about the Convicts Battalion, and if we can, I want to talk about the unit, and I'll -- I'm not going to cut you off. I know that there are just -- there are issues relating to who was in charge of the unit, but nonetheless, I want to come back to the issue of the unit that you thought of as the Convicts Battalion or the Kaznjenicka Bojna. Now, at the very beginning of this section of your cross-examination I showed you the chart that you had marked on when you were a witness for the Defence in the Mladen Naletilic case here at the Tribunal, and I'm going to take you back to that chart which for this trial is marked as P09324, 9324.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we could put it up on the screen also. I think that the part we need to see is the part that bears the General's markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's it, General. I think you've just reached it there in your binder. Now, as we look at this, General, I'm actually going to take you back to your testimony, your sworn testimony in the Naletilic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we've got this on Sanction, Mr. President. We can put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to read you a part of the questions on cross-examination that were put to you by my colleague sitting behind me, Mr. Scott. And this is as we see at page 9690 of the Naletilic, Martinovic transcript. You were asked the following question: "Q. Sir, you've told us several times, I believe, in the last several days that the Convicts Battalion was part of the HVO. Are you changing your answer?" And your response, General, was: "A. No, sir. But the Convicts Battalion, in the form in which I knew about it, except for the first case I mentioned and the Orlovac feature, as its commander appeared Mr. Mario Hrkac and Mr. Andabak, and that was also something I repeated several times. Mr. Mladen Naletilic was not a part of the military structure. Nor do I know him as a commander of this unit in the military part." And then you were asked the next question: "Q. All right, sir. Just so the record is clear then - I don't want to sit down without this being clear - you're not disagreeing - you've not changed your answer that the Convicts Battalion by whoever you say it was commanded by, but you confirm again that the Convicts Battalion was part of the HV -- military HVO; correct?" And you say: "A. Correct, as for the structure of the HVO, which you showed me, and I drew with a marker where the Convicts Battalion was, and I stand by it." So now, General, in this testimony at the very end when you mentioned the structure and you're making markings, what you're doing is referring to this exhibit here, the chart that we're looking at, 9234; correct? That's a yes or no question, General. When you were referring to the markings, are you referring to your markings on this chart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You claim that this question can be answered by a yes or no, and I claim that it cannot. You have left out the most important part. I was talking about the year 1992 and about Orlovac, and then I said that the Convicts Battalion, or, rather, the commander Andabak in Orlovac was within the HVO structure. Between 1992, and that is in May and the beginning of June, and 1993, there is a big difference, and I can't answer with a yes or no, but I stand by what I said then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and what I'm saying now. I don't know -- the exact answer, Mr. Stringer, is I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. I probably would have said the same thing. You're not at all answering the question. You have not noticed what the question was it appears. The question was, I read it here, were you referring -- when you were referring to the markings, are you referring to your marks on this chart? That was the question. The question was not whether you confirmed that the Convicts Battalion was part of the HVO or any substantive part. The question was did you refer to this chart with the markings, and that I do not see how it cannot be answered yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, at the time, I was participating and saying all I know, but if a statement is not quite correct, it doesn't mean that it is false. I came as a Defence witness, unprepared, and I don't know. I'm telling you now I don't know under whose command Mladen Naletilic Tuta was at the time I was on the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will ask Mr. -- perhaps I misquote him. I will ask Mr. Stringer again to put the question to you, because it seems that you did not understand me now. I'm sorry, maybe I have some speech impairment. Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the question is this: Was the HVO -- excuse me. Was the Convicts Battalion a part of the HVO? A simple question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the time you assumed command of the HVO Main Staff, 27 or 24 July 1993, the date you wrote on the chart. Was the Convicts Battalion a part of the HVO at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then -- well, I'm going to put it to you, General. You're not telling us the truth now, because the fact is when you sat here in this Tribunal as a witness under oath in the Naletilic trial, at the same time you wrote this date and made these markings on this chart, you wrote KB up next to the box on professional units. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then so --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- I'm going to put it to you, General, that you're not telling us the truth again today. In fact, the KB was a part of the HVO structures, precisely as you've indicated on the chart that's in evidence from the Naletilic case. Isn't that the case? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, we're talking about two different things in the HVO. I'm talking about the units that come under the command of the Main Staff, and now you're saying that the HVO -- the HVO, of course, is the military police as well. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You keep changing my question to suit yourself. You've got to stop doing that. You've got to answer my question. We have a chart here that is the HVO, all right? Not the Main Staff. We've got Main Staff here. We've got the Defence Department elsewhere. I'm asking you about the HVO, and the fact is, General, that under oath back in the Naletilic trial, I've just read you your testimony, you testified unequivocally that the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO military, the HVO military, and that is in fact how it was; isn't that correct? The Convicts Battalion was, in fact, a part of the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No matter how much you or anyone else tries to get from me something they want, they can make their own statement for the transcript. My clear knowledge is that I was not in command of the Convicts Battalion. What it belonged to, whether it belonged to other --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to direct the witness to answer the question, because he continues to evade by changing the question. Was the Convicts Battalion part of the HVO military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the question put by Mr. Stringer is very clear, especially as he has Mr. Scott behind him, because it was Mr. Scott who put the question to you at the time. We have on the screen, and you see on the screen, the document marked by yourself, and then you indicated Mr. Mate Boban as being the commander of the army. Then you wrote Bruno Stojic as being head of the Defence Department. Then you framed the Main Staff, and you put the date the 27th of July, 1993. And we see that it was you who was the commander of the HVO from the 27th of July. More delicate is what we see on the right. You put ATG and a circle around it and an arrow from which one can make the conclusion that the ATG depended on the Main Staff as professional units. And to the right you have marked KB, the Convicts Battalion. Mr. Scott, at the time when he was questioning you, asked you to confirm whether the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO, and at the time you said yes, but then you gave an explanation that at the time at Orlovac, which was in 1992 and not 1993, the person in command of the Convicts Battalion was not Naletilic, and that to the best of your knowledge Naletilic was in a different structure. Therefore, the conclusion I can make is that in 1992 the Convicts Battalion participated in a military operation under the command of the HVO, but in 1993 not. Just before the break, and I thank my colleague Judge Prandler who tried to explain this, and under oath you're telling us that the Convicts Battalion did not come under the HVO, and you were the commander of the HVO. So that is the situation now. Mr. Stringer is drawing the conclusion that you are lying. That is what he told you when he said that you are not telling the truth, and you say that the Convicts Battalion did not belong to the HVO. In 1992 it did belong, and that's what you've said in the Naletilic case. Now you need to explain to us why with your own hand you marked KB in the presence of Mr. Scott and in the Naletilic case. What exactly does this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the HVO be defined? That is the root of the confusion. Is the HVO the SIS? Is it the IPD? Is it -- I don't know what, doctors. All this is the HVO. The military police is the HVO. Please, Mr. Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must say, Mr. Praljak, this -- your reaction, which is not an answer, but the reaction is not really serious. We did not here ever have problems of what is the HVO. You are again escaping, and you have to answer the questions, precisely answer the questions Mr. Stringer is putting to you. This seems to be very difficult to you. You have been reminded many times of this, and you seem to find it extremely difficult to conform with this, but it is the rules of the game here. You always say that you want a fair trial. This is your part in the fair trial as a witness, that you answer the questions that are put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I would like to appeal -- appeal to you to refrain from psychological characteristics as something being serious or not serious. I would appeal to you to refrain from psychological definitions of my answers. I will complete the testimony as follows: The Convicts Battalion was not in the structure of the command of the Main Staff. We have not defined what the HVO is. You may have done so, but HVO is a broader concept, and there's the Main Staff. Within that HVO and the Main Staff, during my command, the Convicts Battalion was not there. And you can try to imply whatever you wish and to try and trap me. I will not accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I believe that when the Prosecutor says the HVO, the Prosecutor is using the term in the broad sense, and in the broad sense Naletilic was a part the HVO. But when you say the HVO, I think that in your mind it is the military component of the HVO of which you were the commander, and within that military component the Convicts Battalion does not fit within the chain of command. The Convicts Battalion may have been somewhere else within the general HVO, but not within the military structure of which you took the command on the 27th of July, 1993. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct. My complete knowledge is that it was not within the structure of my command. I don't know which other structure it belonged to, but it was probably in the HVO. That is the precise and correct answer. Forgive me, Judge Trechsel. Don't ask me to testify in this way or not, and I'm saying what I know. They were not within the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, leave Judge Trechsel for the moment aside, because we Judges are trying to understand what are you saying. We're trying to understand what you're saying. My understanding now is that when you said in the Naletilic case that the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO, one should conclude from that that you meant in the broader sense, and today you're talking about the military structure, of which you assumed command, that it was not within that structure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceeding from there, Mr. Stringer, take over, please, and develop your arguments. You may not agree with what he says, which is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to say, Mr. Praljak, it's not for you to give me any lessons on how I have to put questions unless I really violate rules, and the term "serious" has not been used in the sense of some psychological meaning but an objective assessment of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
