utterances.text: [Interpretation] What would objective be? What are you talking about objectively? Please, I have every respect for you, but please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no. We're not going to discuss my use of the language further. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the chart P9324, right at the top, it's for the -- the year is indicated 1993. Do you see that, the chart that you wrote on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the date, the 27th of July, 1993, that's written on there. That's what you wrote, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Stringer, but allow me just one thing. If I had not happened to remember that the KB did not stand for the Convicts Battalion for the previous document, then in the previous case, for example, this would've appeared as the Convicts Battalion. You gave me just a couple of minutes to try and remember that this was another brigade, the Knez Branimir brigade. You are giving me things to do without any preparations. You did not give me the document in advance to prepare myself, and this is how things are done. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact -- no --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then in the record of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're not going to run the show. The fact is that you remembered it much better back in the year 2000 when you testified -- or 2002, I should say, and you truthfully indicated in response to Mr. Scott's question that in fact the HVO -- or that the -- that in fact the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO military. Can we agree that that's what you said under oath in the Tuta trial back in 19 -- or back in 2002?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you on anything. On 2003 I was completely unprepared, and now here I worked for years to try and remember the things that I had forgotten in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I don't have in front of me the statement -- or, rather, the reply that Mr. Praljak gave to Mr. Scott's question, but I do not recollect that he mentioned the military structure of the HVO. In the text, it just says "HVO," not the military. Can you verify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you hit the right button, we have the transcript from the Naletilic trial on the screen in Sanction, Mr. President, and it is actually the military structure that's being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. In line 14, and this is very important, it says in English: "Mr. Mladen Naletilic was not a part of the military structure." It's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Except I'm asking about the Convicts Battalion. We can -- for the purposes of this discussion, Mr. President, I'm disregarding who the commander might be. I'm asking about a unit that's well-known, that appears in many of the documents, a unit called the Convicts Battalion, and I'm simply asking the general to confirm what he said back under oath in 2002 which was that the Convicts Battalion fell within the military structure of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the text in front of me. Mr. Scott is asking him, in line 20, and I can be checked by all the English-speaking persons, you say: "Do you confirm that the Convicts Battalion was part of the military HVO," and he adds the word "correct." And Praljak replies: "Correct, but "as for the structure of the HVO...." he doesn't say military structure. So you see, I don't have the French version to be able to compare the two, but in the English version there is Mr. Scott who says to him "military structure," and he answers "structure of the HVO" in line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll just read the rest of the answer in English so that it can be interpreted into the other languages. Line 22 the General says: "Correct. As for the structure of the HVO, which you showed me, and I drew with a marker where the Convicts Battalion was, and I stand by it." And again just for the record, Mr. President, this chart is a schematic overview of the HVO structure in 1993. So I -- so we're putting it to the general --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it to you one final time, General, because I think we've pretty much exhausted this. The fact is that the Convicts Battalion during the period that you were in command of the HVO Main Staff, the Convicts Battalion was a part of the HVO military structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was not under the command of the Main Staff. I don't know where it was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there's any use in pursuing this one any more. I'm ready to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Yes. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I believe you have the next binder there with you. We're going to talk about events just prior to and then during October 1992 and thereafter in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record or for counsel, this is list number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to start off, I'm going to take us back a little bit earlier than October of 1992, back to the 21st of July, 1992, for a little bit of context. This particular transcript, presidential transcript, has been referred to a lot of times throughout the trial. This is a conversation that takes place or a meeting that takes place over about a 12-hour period at the presidential palace, and it's on the day that Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina sign off on the agreement on friendship and cooperation, so that's sort of the background. And I want to take you just to one small part of this and to some of the words of President Izetbegovic. This is on page 35, starting on page 35, at the bottom. President Izetbegovic starts speaking -- I'm sorry. This is P00336, for the record. 336. And President Izetbegovic starts talking at the bottom of page 35 saying that the war started at the moment when they did not have an army. He's talking about the developments. And then the next page, in the middle of the page, he says: "So the spontaneous resistance to the aggressor started, and the people were managing in all possible ways. So it led to establishing in this case of two different formations, the HVO was established in the areas dwelled mostly by the Croatian population, and the TO continued functioning in those other areas." And he continues talking on and he starts talking about problems as between the two. In -- toward the bottom of the page then he says: "In the areas where there are purely -- in purely Croatian areas the HVO is differently politically coloured that in the diverse areas. "In certain areas we have examples of an excellent cooperation of the HVO and the TO up till now, that is, we have the joint commands of some kind, and in some areas we have problems even in that, because on the strength of the HVO, certain political goals appear, goals to create a canton or, according to some people's beliefs, something that even looks like as the state within Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then I'm going to skip down a paragraph. He says: "We simply have very different tendencies within the HVO - loyal ones, so to say, loyal to Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the way to those radical ones who are at the bounds of loyalty, and the question is if they are loyal to Bosnia and Herzegovina at all." And then he continues talking, and he's talking about Croatia's policy in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then the next page with the part I'm mostly interested in for this, on page 38, at the top he says: "We have the cases of civilian authorities which were legally elected on democratic elections being dismissed by the HVO and the establishing of new military departments which naturally we cannot accept." Are you able to follow, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just partly. It would be good if you gave me the page number or the ERN number. This is what I've been asking for. You have been talking and talking and finally you're going to put a question to me, but let's go back to the last thing that you read out. Where is that? I have not been able to find the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Page 38. On these transcripts the English version and the Croatian version are -- are the same. So I'll re-read the last part where Izetbegovic says: "We have the cases of civilian authorities which were legally elected on democratic elections." Do you have that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "Being dismissed by the HVO and the establishing of new military departments, which, naturally, we cannot accept." Then he goes on to talk. He talks about Doboj where the HVO and the TO are acting together and have a Joint Command. And then the next paragraph he says: "There are opposite cases, for example, in Busovaca, or lately in Kiseljak, where the local powerful persons came across an idea to establish even a customs office - as if it is another country, et cetera. And that creates huge political problems." Now, General, you were not present at this meeting on the 21st of July, 1992, and your involvement up until this period of time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as I understand, has been in connection with the liberation of Mostar during June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So at this point in time, General, is it fair to say that you were not familiar with or not involved in activities or developments whereby municipal HVOs were taking over political control of certain municipalities in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are taking this as a fact. However, I can't see where you are quoting from. I don't see Mr. Izetbegovic stating this as a fact. He says there are cases. The only important sentence here is that the war started and he did not have an army. He had been talking to the Serbs all the time, and when the war started --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Turn to the next exhibit, P00382. This is dated 12th of August, 1992. It's a decision on the appointment of the municipal HVO for Prozor, and here we have Dario Kordic signing off on behalf of Mate Boban on a decision purporting to appoint a municipal HVO comprising these individuals. So, General, the question is this: Were you aware that during this period of time, say summer of 1992, the HVO was taking over political control of certain municipalities by forming these municipal HVOs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a little about that. However, as far as I know, the authority in Prozor was divided within the HDZ and the SDA, but this was not based on the victory in the elections but the reciprocity of the votes in the election and the HVO was supposed to assume defence because there was nobody else who was up to the task, up to defending Prozor from the Army of Republika Srpska as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm just asking if you were aware of this, and you're saying you knew a little bit about it. Were you aware that these municipal HVOs were not lawful entities under the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the extent that they replaced the War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was in compliance with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The principle was that an individual, a municipality, and a local commune all had to participate and organise themselves in the matters of defence. The central government did not do anything. They did -- had not been prepared for the war. They had left the country. Well… this… I don’t know. But you've heard this a hundred times. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have indeed heard this a hundred times. You're not asserting, are you, General, that in fact Dario Kordic and Mate Boban possessed legitimate authority under the constitution to appoint individuals to municipal HVOs, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact, but I think that they did have the authority. I believe that Mate Boban did have the authority to organise defence in the places where nobody else could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you say that his authority flowed from the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, this is what I think, but do not assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Turn to the next exhibit. It's P00385. Now, this is dated the same day as the previous exhibit, 12th of August, 1992. So on the day that Dario Kordic for Mate Boban appointed the HVO -- municipal HVO for Prozor, we see that Valentin Coric, who is the head of the military police administration, issues this order, in keeping with the need, as he says, to control the movement of paramilitary formations in Herzegovina, carried out by the Croatian Defence Council. And then he orders that commanders of military police stations in the municipalities of Herzegovina under the control of the HVO, with certain exceptions, issue permits for the movement of vehicles, i.e., BH TO members on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and do so on the basis of their estimation of whether the travel is justifiable. Vehicles of the TO, members are to be stopped if they do not possess the said permit. They are instructed to obtain it. Now, General, were you aware that as of August of 1992, certain elements within the HVO were claiming or asserting that the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a paramilitary formation when it was in the territory of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't see this in the text. This is your interpretation. It -- what it says here is that -- and this applied to the HVO, as you could see, that a member of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to go to his municipality, to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to obtain a paper that allowed him free movement. It doesn't say here that it would be the HVO in those municipalities who provided him with that. It would be the organ in the municipality in charge of that, which in conditions of war is only logical. And this also applied in -- to the Croatian Defence Council. They also had to have -- very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, you're not -- in fact, what this order requires is that the HVO military police issue permits and that TO vehicles have to obtain those permits from the HVO military police. Isn't that what this requires?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say the military police of the HVO? I can't see that. Could you please refer me to the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read it to you. Coric orders: "That commanders of military police stations of the municipalities of Herzegovina under the control of the HVO, with the exception of Mostar, Konjic, Jablanica, and Gornji Vakuf, issue permits for the movement of vehicles, i.e., BH TO members on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And then I'll skip down and he says: "Vehicles of the BH Territorial Defence, that is, BH TO members are to be stopped if they do not possess the said permit ..." Right? So Coric here is, in fact, directing that TO personnel within various parts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna have to be in possession of permits issued by the HVO military police. Isn't that what this says?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police of the municipality, but that doesn't apply to Mostar, Konjic, Jablanica, and Gornji Vakuf where they were mixed compositions. What this is about is a desire to prevent smuggling and all the other types of crimes that started appearing at the time. The same applied to every member of the HVO who wanted to move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, it's not about smuggling. We know what it's about. It says right here at the top. It's about the need to control the movement of paramilitary formations in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say paramilitary, sir? Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I would just like to help everybody and point to an error in the English translation. I believe that's the origin of the problem because in the English translation in the title it says paramilitary formations, whereas in the original it says military formations. There's no reference to paramilitary formations in the original. General Praljak may be allowed to read the sentence preceding the title because I believe that this sentence is the root of the problem. The English translation is wrong. And since I'm on my feet, I believe that the mistake is important, and I believe that my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, would be well-advised to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll have that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, why don't you read it to us? I'm not going to challenge or dispute what counsel's just said. Read the introductory two lines there that begin with the words "In keeping with."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "In keeping with the need to control the movement of military formations in the areas of Herzegovina under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, I hereby issue the following order." This means that this applies to all military formations and bringing order to the area. There is no reference to any paramilitaries. And as far as I remember, there was an identical order in place for the HVO, as far as I can remember. I believe I saw is it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, then, it's the HVO military police. Except for these four municipalities, it's the HVO military police that's going to issue permits and thereby assure control over the passage of the BH Territorial Defence within those territories; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you -- you keep on adding things. First of all, this applies only to the areas of Herzegovina and only the municipalities under the control of the HVO. The municipalities with mixed population have been excluded, Konjic and Jablanica, for example. Such permits there were issued either by the TO or the BiH Army. This is where 10.000 wounded pass through. Over several millions of people pass though areas for crying out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back to the previous document, P00382, which again is from the 12th of August, 1992. Because we know, General, that beginning from October of 1992 and throughout the remainder of the time that you became or were associated with the HVO, until November of 1993, you spent a lot of time in the area of Prozor. The individuals who have been appointed here by Mr. Boban or Kordic acting on his behalf, did you know at any time or did you have dealings with Ilija Petrovic beginning in October of 1992? And I'll ask you the same question for Ilija Franjic, commander of the HVO Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all -- first of all, Mr. Stringer, I reject the whole introduction and your assertions as relevant, because they're nothing but your assertions, nothing more, and my answer to your question has nothing whatsoever to do with your assertions. I did know Ilija Petrovic, and I also knew Ilija Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You knew him in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him when I arrived in Rama-Prozor after the clash that broke out up there. I met both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did those two individuals maintain these positions within the HVO organisation, to the best of your knowledge, until the 9th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next item, General, I want to take you to a little bit of testimony that we heard in this trial. It was quite a long time ago. It was the testimony of Mr. Omer Hujdur. He testified in this trial on the 20th of June, 2006. We're going to put his picture up in Sanction. Maybe you'll see it on the screen and it will help you recognise him. And again, this relates to certain HVO political activities in the Prozor area prior to and after the conflict there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I'm looking at the photograph and I can see that the blinds have been lowered behind him. I don't know if protective measures were in place or not, but could you perhaps check that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I did check it, Your Honour, and he is -- he testified publicly. His testimony is not protected. I don't know why the blinds are down in the photo. Actually, he requested protective measures. They were not granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, on the 6th of June, I'm going to ask you -- or I'm going to read you a little bit of his testimony about the school curriculum in Prozor. This is an area where you spent part of your time when you were young. I want to ask you if you had any information about these issues in your dealings in Prozor. And this is at page 3496 of the transcript, which we can also put up on the screen so people can follow along. He says the question at line 12: "Q. When did this new school year start or was it scheduled to start?" And the answer is that: "A. It was supposed to start, to the best of my recollection, on the 7th of September, but the school year didn't resume then until the attack on Prozor and it continued without the Bosniaks but much later on. So it was just discontinued." And then the question: "Q. To conclude on the topic the school curriculum, when the school year did resume after the attack on Prozor, was that with the Croatian curriculum?" And says: "A. Yes." And then question: "Q. At that stage, now we're talking November or December 1992, were any of your children subjected to this new curriculum?" And the answer is: "A. Yes. That was the time -- I apologise. Excuse me." And I'm going to skip over. He talks about the things that happened in Prozor. So I'll move to the next page. And he says on line 5: "A. There was intensive activity to have the people who left Prozor return. Unfortunately, the people did return, but when they returned, and I hope we'll have enough time to discuss that, too, the school was organised." He says: "A. My wife also returned. She was pregnant at the time. She was four months pregnant, and she had to -- we already had two children -- or, rather, she returned with two children, and one of them was supposed to go to sixth form. And the first day he went to school, after being introduced, he was told, after he stated his name and surname, that he should say that his homeland was Herceg-Bosna and that the capital city of his homeland was Mostar. Of course, the child could not accept that, and his answer was to say that his homeland was Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the capital was Sarajevo. When he said that and when she insisted, there was a conflict that I don't want to talk about." Now, General, were you aware of the introduction of an exclusively Croatian or Croat curriculum in the schools in Prozor at or after the events that occurred there in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, but I do know that many people had already returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- thanks to action that I had taken, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The next exhibit, just for purposes of the time-frame, P00570, because we'll see this -- this document's dated the 10th of October, 1992, not long before you came down to Prozor. And so just so we all recall, General, you at this date were appointed by President Tudjman to the position of assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a lot earlier, sir. This is some other document or something has been changed and it was necessary to draft it again, but I became the assistant minister of defence in March 1992. I don't know what's been modified here exactly or why this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, so that when you did arrive in Prozor in October of 1992, you did hold the position of assistant minister of defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the next exhibit is P00608. This is a report of the SIS, HVO Tomislavgrad. This is the chief of security, Luka Markesic. We've seen a number of his reports in this case, General, and here he's talking about the situation in the town. Now, this is Prozor, 20th of October, and he says: "The situation in town is deteriorating. "After the hoisting of the Croatian flag on the police station, there is a possibility that large-scale clashes will occur in the town." So, General, first of all just so we all recall, when specifically did you arrive in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some document it says he arrived on the 20 -- the 26th, 7th, 8th. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. You were sent by President Tudjman, as I understand it, with the mandate to prevent a war or a conflict from breaking out. Is that in general what your mandate was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. The conflict had already broken out. There was an agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic, and I was requested to go down there to solve the situation to the extent it was possible to calm things down, to make the situation tolerable, and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were aware or were you in the aware that prior to your arrival an HVO Municipal Staff had been appointed by Dario Kordic for Mate Boban, a Croatian flag had been erected at the police station, and that there was a very tense situation in Prozor as a result of these activities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived there, naturally I didn't have sufficient information at my disposal, but subsequently, naturally I tried to find out why a conflict had broken out, and naturally as usual you have had a look at only two documents. You didn't have a look at 20 documents drafted by Luka Marketic [as interpreted], but who tried to produce a conflict, how did it develop, how did it develop, and -- there was a spark that ignited everything when the ABiH killed one or two Croats for no reason at a check-point for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you know, to hear your version of the events, if there are any tensions in these areas, whether it's Prozor or Gornji Vakuf or elsewhere, it's always just because the ABiH -- the armies down there are causing tension and the HVO is not doing anything to contribute to the tension. The fact is that the HVO by its political takeover, as we've seen here in Prozor, by raising the Croatian flag and by engaging in other activities such as that, that's the reason why the tensions were running so high in these areas like Prozor in October of 1992; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- let me tell you something --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to continue with this. There was --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- a political objective on the part of the HVO to take political authority over in these municipalities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and of course you and Tudjman and everybody on the HVO side wanted to avoid a war with the Muslims, but the fact is that the war resulted and was resorted to by the HVO because it realised that it could not achieve these political goals without going to war. Isn't that really what started in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing you have said is true. This is just your desire to represent things in this way. Then there are documents that support this. The HVO, the HDZ didn't have to conquer anything in Rama. They had won in the election, Mr. Stringer, and people down there were simply the members of a constituent people. When Alija Izetbegovic said that they didn't even want cantons, they wanted some kind of cantons. Well, imagine that. He said, “If you don't accept my unitary state, if you want cantons, well, then you are traitors, good for nothing.” Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're asserting that because they won election in Prozor they had the right to throw the constitution out the window and appoint a municipal HVO instead of a war presidency under the constitution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect, Mr. Stringer. We've read through the constitution here on a number of occasions. This has been explained several times. Apart from not preparing for war, Mr. Tudjman [as interpreted] was performing his duties in an unconstitutional way. He drafted a constitution in an unconstitutional way. You're not interested in this, however, so please continue. I will answer your questions peacefully. In Rama, the division of power that I became aware of was the division of power between the Croats and the Muslims on the basis proportionality, and at a meeting that they had in order to solve certain issues, this killing occurred and then conflict broke out. I did my work to the best of my ability and I was quite successful, and I didn't opt for either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think there's a correction that needs to be made in the transcript, Mr. President, although I don't know whether the mistake was by the witness or by the interpreters. Line -- beginning on line 18 it reads that the general said that: "This has been explained several times. Apart from not preparing for war, Mr. Tudjman was performing his duties in an unconstitutional way, drafted a constitution in an unconstitutional way." I think that the general was not referring to President Tudjman there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, General. P00602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a question that is very important and that requires additional explanation. Mr. Stringer says the political objective was to take control of the municipalities, and in order to do so it was necessary to have a recourse to war, to go to war. So that's what he thinks. That's his thesis. Then there was the event in Prozor, and we know that you were down there. I'm trying to understand your arrival there in the light of the Prosecution's theory. If the Prosecution is right, then someone decided on political control, either Mate Boban, someone else, or Zagreb, political control such as shown to you by the Prosecution. There were appointments in this well-known document. Well, we can consider that this document supports this thesis. And then we have just seen an interesting document, another interesting document that shows that the issue of the flag gave rise to certain problems. So according to the Prosecution's scenario, there was a decision to take political power, the implementation via the document. We've seen appointments, then there was action that was taken. The flag was hoisted and then certain events transpired. At that point you arrived, you subsequently arrived as you have said in order to calm things down, have people released, so on and so forth. On that basis, a reasonable Judge might ask himself within what kind of a context did Mr. Praljak arrive there if there was such a political objective on the tables. What was the reason for his arrival within the framework of his objective. Given Mr. Stringer's thesis that you contest, well, there are documents nevertheless, and it's necessary to provide explanations with regard to the documents because the documents tend to support the claims made by Mr. Stringer. So how do you explain the fact that one decided to appoint individuals and municipalities whereas in theory it would have been natural to hold elections for such appointments? How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a complex, a large case. I understand this. But to explain this problem, we've had a look at 40 relevant documents. We've admitted 40 relevant documents to see who was involved, who fled from the lines, when and where, how people were arming themselves in secret, how they wouldn't accept authority and so on. There is this appointment of a certain military I-don’t-know-what and so on. Down there, as far as I know, this is the information I was provided with, and there was a government that didn't even abide by regular democratic rules in the west. In the west when a party wins an election they form a government, but that wasn't the case down there. The power was shared, well, let's say by the HDZ, the Croatian party, and the SDA, the Muslim party, on the basis of the number of votes won in the election. There were two political options. The unitary policies for Bosnia and Herzegovina and the policies for the rights of the Croatian people, and people thought that this was relevant, that they should decide on the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Alija Izetbegovic couldn't decide on internal matters. He was granted the borders, but a constitute -- a constituent sovereign people has the right to discuss the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the first thing. And the second thing is that I arrived actually in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have to stop you there because you start answering the question and then you go off on a tangent and deal with another area. You have just provided an answer that might be satisfactory. With regard to the documents, you say certain individuals were appointed for military reasons because the municipality of Prozor, if I have understood this correctly, wasn't playing according to the rules so you intervened. That's a satisfactory answer. Why then move into other areas, go off on a tangent. Try to restrict yourself. Try to limit yourself to very precise answers, otherwise the answer that you do provide and that might have probative value gets completely submerged by other arguments that are not so relevant. So I put to you a question. I asked you why this document which seems to support the Prosecution's thesis about the takeover of the political power is of such and such a nature, and you say, No these are military appointments and you explain why. Very well. And then you stop there because otherwise your answer will get lost in other comments and everyone will say it's difficult to understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand what you're saying. I know I times go too far because I always have the impression -- well, as I have said, partiality kills me. But as far as your second question is concerned, I was sent or requested -- sent, however you want to put it. Tudjman put his fist down on the table after discussing matters with Alija Izetbegovic. He said go down there. We don't want to go to war with the Muslims. We don't need a war and so on and so forth. But let's be realistic, and in a month and a half I did what we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can't be of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, four lines are sufficient to answer my question. First of all, you can say Tudjman sent me down there saying we didn't want to go to war with the Muslims, that would be one line; and then, secondly, you can say this document concerned military appointments because the others didn't want to play by the rules and that would be it. There we have it. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I think it would be good to avoid misunderstandings to state following: General Praljak didn't say that this document, signed by Mr. Kordic on behalf of Mate Boban, amounted to appointing military commanders. I don't want to -- it to appear as if the general gave false testimony. If you have a look at P382, you can see that it concerns appointing members of the civilian HVO in Prozor, and the penultimate individual referred to is the commander of the municipal headquarters, the military component of the HVO. I just want to be very precise to avoid problems at a later stage of the proceedings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we've just been looking at P00608, which is the Markesic report on the effect of the hoisting of the Croatian flag. Now, on the same day another thing happened in Prozor that might have impacted the tensions, and it's your next document, P00602. And what we see, General, is that on this day Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic issued an order to block all roads immediately, and this is an order that's being issued to the Prozor HVO, Gornji Vakuf HVO. And we see the HVO of the other municipalities. "Use all available forces to stop the TO units that are moving towards Travnik." So it made a report on the situation in your territory. Now, we know that events or conflicts between the HVO and the TO or the ABiH did take place in Central Bosnia at or about this time. So again, General, the fact is that in Prozor, again prior to the time you arrived, what we've seen is the HVO taking or purporting to take over the civilian or political control of Prozor. We've seen attempts to hoist the Croatian flag in Prozor, and now we're seeing that the HVO is going to block TO units in these municipalities, including Prozor, and to prevent them from moving toward Travnik. So again we have another situation in which the HVO is essentially asserting control over Prozor municipality. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you are providing us with an incredible number of theses yet again. I'll just try to answer now and tell you something about these theses. I dispute all of them. Even if they're correct or incorrect, I don't think this manner of examining me is correct. I consider it quite normal to raise the Croatian flag --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I apologise for interrupting you. The answer could be very simple. We have a document from General Petkovic. It says block all forces moving in the direction of Travnik. It's a military document from a military authority. It has nothing to do with political objectives, and it requires a military response a priori, and instead of responding in military terms you go off into a different area. Sometimes I ask myself whether you understand the question put to you by the Prosecution, because the question in this case is extremely simple. He says here you have a document that shows that many documents were taken for political control. It's a military document. You can say, No, you're mistaken because in Travnik there were the BH forces. We didn't want there to be significant units there, so we freeze the men there, and that's why the order is here. I thought that's what you say, but you went off on a tangent. So before answering a question, try to understand the question put to you and then answer. I know you're an accused. You say the question is put to sort of trap me. Perhaps but perhaps not. It's to explain the nature of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, if such a question was put to me, I would clearly answer. I have no idea what this document is about. In those days my only role was to calm the situation, but read the expose by Mr. Stringer. You hung up the flag, which means you should be killed. You're at fault for doing this. This is a crime. It's not a crime for a Croat to hoist a Croatian flag. So please read the introduction in which he makes three points and then fourthly he doesn't ask me anything. And my answer, my simple answer to this document, is I have no idea what this is about. I think a Croatian flag can be hoisted where we are a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you could have said straight away that you know nothing about this document. That's what you should have said. But, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the point is, General, that in fact a good deal of things were going on in Prozor before you arrived that you didn't know about apparently. Isn't that so? You didn't know about the flag, did you? You didn't know about the blocking of roads here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer. You asked two questions, the flag and the road. The answer was no, but we do not know whether it's no to both or to one or to other. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. It would have been -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- may I invite you to divide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know about the flag incident that Luka Markesic is reporting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, and I don't agree with the word "incident."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the fact is that if the tensions in Prozor are high and if in fact so high that conflict breaks out, as you said, for whatever reason, you don't know to what extent the HVO's own conduct contributed to that, do you, because you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I arrived there, I did not know. After that, I learnt more or less everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next exhibit is P00628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, regarding the question of the flag, you expressed your view point a moment ago. I listened to you, and I am obliged to put to you the following question: You are aware of the importance of flags on mentalities. You know that sometimes when an X hoists a flag that Y don't like, this can cause a series of events. Let me remind you of Borovo Selo. So what would be interesting is to know whether at the level of the HVO, the military component, were there any precise orders in one way or another regarding the hoisting of flags? Were Croats encouraged to hoist flags on municipal buildings or their windows in their houses, or was there no such order? And these were just local individuals who would decide, Look, let's hoist the flag because it is our -- something that characterises us. Because a flag sometimes is an element that can trigger a whole series of events. Were there any orders, or were there individuals who simply decided to hoist flags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no orders, as far as I know, and I did not issue any such order, and there were no such orders, only, I believe, that no one should have been prevented from doing this if that is what he wanted to do. In 1992, I personally, and Luburic, as you saw from the documents, distributed to the BH Army the lilies, their flags, for them to bear them on their sleeves, for them to be equal, to feel equal, and you can see from their press reports that this was done throughout 1992. Love your own and respect other peoples. However, on the other side this was not respected, this principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have answered. There were no orders to that effect. So it's in the transcript. It's time for the break, and Mr. Stringer will continue afterwards, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document I'd like to take you to is P00628. P00628. Oh, I see you have it. Okay. Dated 23 of October, 1992. And this is from the HVO Presidency Prozor. It bears a number of signatures. I can't tell who they are, but in any event, this is directed to the Muslim military and civilian representatives in Prozor municipality. The subject is "Our Proposals for Overcoming the Newly Arisen Political and Security Situation." And in these five points the HVO Presidency and HVO command lay out their demands, if I can put it that way, or requirements to the Muslim military and civilian representatives, which include an urgent and unconditional cessation of all military operations. They are insisting on the HVO soldiers being dispatched to fight at the front line against the Serbs. Number 3 is a --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. "Your soldiers," the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. I stand corrected. This is the HVO demanding that the ABiH send soldiers to the front line, that -- number 3 is -- requires a withdrawal of ABiH armed units from the town. Item 4 requires: "Passage for the military police units coming from outside our municipality on their way to their final destination as per their combat task." And then fifthly, they insist on urgent and instant acceptance of civilian and military structure of the HVO HZ HB in which Muslim representatives will also participate proportionally. Now, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must say there's a lot of talking going on and I must say it's quite a distraction. I'm hearing a number of voices from the other side of the room and it's just hard to do this. It's hard enough without having additional distraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The first question, General, is were you familiar with this document at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Petkovic asked for the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the fact that General Petkovic did wish to draw my attention to an error, I assume it's an error in the translation. Colleague Stringer, on page 75, line 8, and it has to do with item 3 of this document. There's no reference to units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Croatian or the English text, but, rather, it says that all armed units need to be withdrawn from the town. So the English text is okay, but in line 8 Mr. Stringer mentions the withdrawal of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is not a correct interpretation of the document, and that is what my client wanted to draw my attention to and asked me to intervene. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, and again I apologise for that. It simply says: "Withdrawal of all armed units from the town." It does not indicate which armed units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, the first question is -- is whether you were aware of this document or if you became aware of this document at the time you arrived in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt subsequently about all their proposals and the events and facts, and as far as I can recollect, I think I was aware of this, too, but this was later when the situation calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in fact there was an escalation, a further escalation of the conflict after this document was issued on the 23rd of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There's a demand for a cessation of hostilities. The conflict had already started. This was not before the conflict but probably on the evening of the 23rd when the conflict -- I can't say exactly, but it says here that the conflict had already started. And they are addressing themselves to the military and civilian representatives of the Muslims in Prozor municipality because they had military and civilian structures just like the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In this document they're insisting that the HVO civilian and military structures be accepted by the Muslim military and civilian; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that here, but it is important to note that the Muslims should participate proportionately. And from this it is evident that the desire was to build a multi-ethnic state in proportion with the population composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Within the structure of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here. That is how the HVO -- they had such units in Mostar, just as the HVO was subordinated in Tuzla, Brcko, and elsewhere. Let's not go into that. We've already talked about that. This was a war, and a good structure could have been built in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, General, did the Muslim civilian and military representatives in Prozor accept these terms or did they reject them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, later on much of this was accepted up to 1993, and there were two separate structures which collaborated. So they went to the common front line again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll talk about what happened then in the subsequent weeks and months. The next document is P00642. Now, General, this one's dated the 24th of October, and it's an order from Colonel Siljeg on control of the territory. I put it to you, General, that this is an attack order of the HVO, directing that all armed forces -- or that the Rama Brigade put all armed forces in Prozor municipality and the town of Prozor itself under the command of the Rama Brigade of the HVO forces, eliminate all combat activities against HVO forces, and then the document continues, and we can all read that. So now, General, in fact this would indicate that in fact the civilian and the military representatives of the Muslims did not, did not accept the demands of the municipal HVO that are contained in the previous document that we were looking at, number 628; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know, this is quite a different matter. There was a conflict, and from the documents shown to this Tribunal, and as far as I know the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was preparing for an attack on Prozor. Before the conflict they had an elaborate plan about this. The Tribunal has those documents, and the Trial Chamber can judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you're saying you don't know whether this results from the acceptance or refusal by the Muslim authorities of those conditions that were set out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the connection between those two documents. I don't see that connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The next document is P00647. Now, this is a report directed to Colonel Siljeg on the situation in the field up to now, 1810 hours, 24th of October, 1992. This is a commander, Major Jure Smidt who is reporting, and he says: "Constant combat activity at the town of Prozor and Rama Lake are under the control of the Prozor HVO" --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- right. We have in the translation here a reference to HV, which is not correct. It's HVO. These two areas are ethnically pure. The Muslim population has been detained or has fled. Now, General, this would strongly suggest, wouldn't it, that in fact combat activities were taking place in Prozor and Rama Lake during the day of the 24th of October up until at least 1810 hours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. What it says here in the document is what it says. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you don't have any reason to dispute this, do you, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I don't know anything about something I can neither dispute nor confirm it. Lack of knowledge is simply lack of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you said that you knew -- know nothing about the document, but that doesn't mean that you cannot express your point of view about that document. You're refusing to do that. Fine, but you are here in an effort to establish the truth. That is what you told us. All the more reason. There's a terrible sentence in this document. You must understand me. I listened to the Prosecutor putting the question to you. You say you don't know the document, and then the Prosecutor moves on to something else. And when the Judges start deliberating, what are they going to say? "Look, in line 3, this is what it says: There are two areas that are ethnically pure. The Muslim population has fled or has been detained." So a reasonable Judge who doesn't go to the bottom of things but is satisfied with what he sees in front of him, can come to a conclusion. Try to explain why the sentence is in this document, why the author of this document makes reference to areas that are ethnically pure, which we are at the heart of the criminal enterprise. You simply say, "I don't know this document," and you say nothing about it. That's fine, but you see, that can have a very significant impact, and as a Judge I must draw your attention to this. Careful, here. There is an incriminating sentence. It would be better for you to respond. It's up to you to give us an answer. First of all, who is the author of this document? You perhaps don't know, et cetera. Perhaps you have something to say about it, because you are here in an effort to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. If the question had been put in that way, I would have provided an answer. When I try to give an answer, I'm interrupted. Jure Smidt is a German with German citizenship who could hardly speak. Jure Smidt was later killed. I met him briefly. He could barely speak Croatian. How he compiled this, I don't know. And I claim that he has no idea what ethnic cleansing is. He probably wanted to say that the population there had been detained during the fighting or had fled, and for them -- for him that is ethnic cleansing. The population detained during the fighting, later on I released all those people from the remand detention. I think it was remand, a number fled. And we can see from this who is attacking who and who fled from whom. Ninety per cent of those who had fled, of course, from the fighting returned, and all the prisoners were released. All the detainees were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. General Praljak, you see the document, and you see that it is addressed to Colonel Siljeg in person. One may, perhaps, think that there is a connection between Smidt and Colonel Siljeg. He is reporting on the situation at 1810 hours, and he adds an assessment regarding the ethnic issue. Perhaps -- this is a hypothesis: Perhaps before there was some communication between Siljeg and this one to deal with this problem, and he is faithfully reporting. He's a soldier executing orders. Perhaps it is false, but someone could say, Look, he is answering perhaps in response to a request from his superior, and perhaps he received an order prior to this, and therefore a reply is necessary. You're telling us he's German. He didn't speak the language. He maybe made a mistake. Maybe, but you must note that this document was communicated by Paket, and another soldier, a Croat, may have drafted the text, and he may have just given instructions, and the soldier may have added something. Everything is possible, because during fighting the leaders are on the front line. They don't stand next to the people at the teleprinter to see what they are writing. So maybe this soldier may have added something to this. I don't know. I wasn't there. But if you are -- limit yourself to saying to Mr. Stringer, I don't know this document without entering into the substance, I am saying that you must pay attention. You must be careful. So your response is to say that this is a German who doesn't know the language, and this explains the words used. But, again, if Colonel Siljeg were to be in front of me, I could say to him, Colonel, you received this from a subordinate. He speaks of ethnic cleansing. He is responding to a request from you or not. If Colonel Siljeg says to me, "I didn't say anything to that effect," then would I say, "How come that you didn't call the person and demand an explanation from him?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Before the answer, I would like only to add it is rather - although a technical question - but since Judge Antonetti mentioned that he -- I mean Smidt cannot speak Croatian, I would like to draw our attention to the fact that there is the -- I believe the original handwriting here attached in Croatian, which seems to me written by -- by Jure Smidt, and of course it might have been not exactly correct in Croatian, but it is up to those who speak Croatian to judge, but anyway, he was in my view, then, somebody who came from Germany and fought alongside the HVO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that his knowledge of Croatian, and I spoke to him once, in my view was not good. He did not use proper words. He says the areas are ethnically. In other words, this is what happened to Muslims. But look here, and I quote, towards the end, "Due to the newly arisen situation, every conversation with the representatives of the TO is impossible." First of all, there were attempts to talk to the TO. And then the last sentence which says: "We will try to get through to Bugojno during the night in order to talk to them, in other words, to establish physical contact with the representatives of the TO." During the conflict, obviously every possible communication with the representatives of the TO was interrupted, but he wanted to go to Bugojno to talk to the TO because in Bugojno the situation between the HVO and the TO at that moment was brilliant. That's why I'm saying that one should look at the whole document. And I believe that his knowledge of Croatian implies that he didn't know what the term "ethnic cleansing" meant for the purpose of a courtroom situation. This is my interpretation of this document. Whether it's correct or not I can't be sure because Smidt is dead. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall then stop here. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, in this case on the 1st of November, 2006, you cross-examined the witness Fahrudin Agic, and in your cross-examination of him, this is page 9396 of the transcript, you put it to him -- you said to him: "Do you know that immediately after the conflict in Prozor I went to that territory?" And he said: "No." And then you said: "Do you know that after that event I stayed until the 24th of December, 1992, in the area of Rama and Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, and Travnik?" And then he says: "Yes, because on the 4th of December you were at a meeting in Gornji Vakuf at Bozo Rajic." So, General, from your own words here you've indicated to us that you arrived in Prozor immediately -- or that you went to Prozor immediately after the conflict there, and that you stayed in that area, in this area that I've just read to you, until the 24th of December. Do you recall that -- that statement on your part?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. That's correct. But what is the meaning of the words "immediately after the conflict"? I first went to Mostar and then -- please, what is the meaning the words "immediately thereafter"? What does it mean immediately after the conflict? How many days after the conflict do you claim that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to fence with you. Let me follow up with some questions. That's how it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. I'm amazed at your question, Mr. Praljak, because you used this term "immediately afterwards," so you must know what you meant when you said it. Normally you don't like others to interpret you. So do you know what you meant when you said "immediately"? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're looking at these documents from the 24th of October, 1992, the last two documents, Siljeg's order on control of the territory, and then the report of Jurgen Smidt that's received or issued on the 24th at 1810 hours. General, the 24th of October is a day when there were extensive military operations conducted by the HVO, resulting in Muslims, as indicated in these areas, Prozor and Rama Lake, being detained or fleeing from the HVO; isn't that true? Did that occur, on the 24th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. Actually, when I ask a question of a witness, I would appreciate if you give the witness the opportunity to answer. I asked the witness what he meant when he said that immediately after the conflict he went to Prozor. I want him to tell me what he meant was immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th or the 28th or the 29th October, 1993. Excuse me. Yes, 1992. I can't remember exactly. You will find it in a document that we saw in this courtroom where it says that Praljak arrived and I was up there with the Muslims. There are several documents to that effect. That's why I -- if somebody had told me this is what I'm going to ask you, then I would have prepared the date and we would have avoided any sort of confusion. It was possibly the 24th, but it's not correct. The 25th is not correct either. That's why I'm insisting on precision as far as that is possible. Unfortunately, it seems that we cannot arrive at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on, Mr. Stringer. I apologise for interrupting, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P00653. 653. This is dated the 26th of October, 1992, and this is a report of the -- a Military Intelligence Service person named Zarko Keza, and it's directed to the head of the Defence Department, Bruno Stojic, personally, General Bobetko, personally, HVO Main Staff Brigadier Petkovic, personally, and IPD AB [phoen] Rajic personally. And this is intelligence -- an intelligence report on the Prozor sector, and it says here -- now we're talking about the 25th of October, the next day. It says: "... fighting was conducted during the day as well with Muslim extremist forces in the Prozor sector. At about 1500 hours, the HVO took control of the old tower near the town, so the whole town is under HVO control. The losses on our side include two dead and seven wound and nobody has been taken prisoners. The losses on the Muslim side have not yet been established, but they are estimated to amount up to a hundred. "The HVO controls the entire area around lake Rama, the town of Prozor, the dam at the lake, the hydroelectric power plant, and the road to Jablanica up until Jasen settlement." Now, General, this -- would you agree with me -- I'm just trying to sort of set the context for the time of your arrival. We've just seen some documents relating to combat or what appear to be combat activities of the 24th of October. Now, this report, would you agree with me, indicates that there was continued fighting on the 25th of October which culminated in the HVO taking the entire town and these other places indicated under control? Can we agree that that was the situation after the 25th of October 1992? Do you know or do you not know? Is this not -- is this not anything you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that, no. I was not familiar with the situation on the 25th, sir, because I wasn't up there. I can't say that it was either this or that or that it wasn't this or that. The only thing I can say, though, is that the number of killed Muslims was two more than the killed in the -- on the HVO side in this conflict, but you have a document to that effect signed by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the time you arrived in Prozor, was the HVO in control of the whole town of Prozor as is indicated here on the 26th or the 25th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you arrived was the HVO also controlling the entire area around Lake Rama as well, as is indicated in this report on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that area as well, but you should know that that area was composed of 90 per cent Croats, as far as I know. There were only one or two smaller hamlets that were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you arrived was the HVO also in control of the area here, indicated the dam at the lake and the hydroelectric power plant at Marina Pecina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the dam certainly. There was a road across the dam that one could use to cross, and as for the hydroelectric plant I really don't know. I can't tell you exactly because I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the time you arrived you know -- or did you find as indicated here that the HVO was in control of the road to Jablanica up until Jasen settlement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact place, but my first attempt to enter Prozor was from Jablanica where I had my first big meeting with some of the Muslim leaderships that had fled Prozor together with Arif Pasalic. It was then when I ride to break through towards Rama using that road. Unfortunately, I was shot at. I don't know who it was, but fire was opened on me. I had to return and take another road. Pasalic and I had to return, although he had not wanted to go to Prozor with me. And then I said, okay, I'll return and then I'll come back alone. That's why I returned to Tomislavgrad and used Salvation Road, and it was a very, very long journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this document that's coming from the Military Intelligence Service and is reporting to the persons indicated on the -- at the back of it. Now, General, in October of 1992 when you went to Prozor and became involved or -- or observed what was going on down there, were you aware that the Military Intelligence Service of the HVO was reporting directly to General Bobetko, at least in respect of this incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I did not go to observe the situation. I went there to bring order to the situation. Secondly, this document doesn't say that the intelligence service reported to Bobetko. It only refers to him as a person who was informed within the scope of the collaboration between the armies about a conflict, which I believe was a logical thing to do between intelligence services -- it was logical for the commander of the southern front in the direction of Dubrovnik to know that there had been conflicts between the BH Army and the HVO that might have reflected negatively in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this Military Intelligence Service, do you know, in October of 1992, was it a part of the HVO Main Staff or was it a part of the Defence Department, or did it -- was it located in a different part of the structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the principles, VOS is a Military Intelligence Service and it is within the structure of the Main Staff for as long as I was there at least. It says here in the heading the Main Staff HVO VOS. Therefore, this is what it says and I really can't tell you more than you can read yourself. In any case, VOS was a military intelligence service and was part of the structure of the Main Staff of the HVO, at least for as long as I was in charge down there, for as long as I was commander down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I have a follow-up question. This document, in my view, is a very important document, just like the one that we saw a little while ago, and you understand it and I'm trying to determine who started the conflict, because if we know that, we can maybe draw a conclusion in respect of the criminal enterprise. To be very clear, and this is your favourite expression, if there was a criminal enterprise in place, we can understand that in October 1992 the HVO launched an operation, captured Muslims, and so on and so forth. This is a view that one can gain from the document. And then there could be another view of the same situation. We have documents that all originate from the intelligence service of the military, I don't know the value of the military service's -- intelligence services of the HVO, but I assume that like any other intelligence service they tried to do their job well and that they tried to inform the authorities in the most precise way. In other words, the author of this document, if there had been a plan for a military operation, I suppose that military intelligence would not be aware of that, because afterwards they had to explain what had happened and how things developed. When we're looking at this document very attentively, as I have for the past ten minutes, what can I conclude? I conclude that this is a report on the events, and it says here, that's in the text, that Muslims had planned an attack in reality. "We were informed that Muslim forces had planned an attack on Prozor in the afternoon on the 24th of October." This is what it says in the document. And then there is a reference to the killing of an HVO soldier and some other consequences. The document speaks in very great detail of the geography of the area where the situation happened, and the author makes a distinction between the villages where there were Muslim extremists and the villages where there was a Muslim control, but nothing happened there in -- in the letter. In the extremist villages which you have listed here, Scipe, Voljavica, Here, Kute, and it says here that the Muslim forces had launched an attack in the direction of Borova Ravan and Pridvorci. In other words, this document that originates from the military intelligence, unless they are telling lies, could create an idea that Prozor had been attacked by the Muslims and that the HVO responded, that they replied. Very well. What I would like to know is this: You were the commander of the HVO, maybe not at the time because you arrived later, you were not there; however, when you were indeed the commander of the HVO, did you have or receive information from the intelligence service, did they do their job in a classical way, or did they respond to very precise orders? How do you remember the intelligence services at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military Intelligence Service had to provide precise, correct, neutral information. Incorrect information can do nothing but bring you to a lost battle or a badly planned battle. I received information that day that they were privy to regularly. The information was collected in different manners. I would be privy to that information. And I believe that insofar as I know, Mr. Zarko Kezo did his job well. This would be the answer, the answer to your first question. Second of all, after I arrived there I learned exactly how things were done. There was - and you have papers to that effect- there was a plan in place where it says that the centre of Prozor should be taken from the BH Army from the direction of Konjic. There was a plan that concerned the Chetniks. Your Honours, things grew little by little. First of all, they took salaries from the HVO and they did not fight the Chetniks. There were protests against that. Then they demanded weapons that were then stored in some depots. I know exactly. There was a meeting between the representatives of the BH Army and the HVO that should have resolved all the unresolved issues, and then there were some snipers on the part of the BH Army that were turned towards people. At the meeting, there was a killing, and everything -- all hell broke loose on the 23rd. That young man from the HVO was killed, and then the situation escalated after problems had mounted for months, and things ended the way they did. Here, Kute, that you see here for a year or a year later attacked Uzdol and killed 40 people there. I was there at the time. I prevented any further retaliation. Unfortunately, however much I'm trying to give you a simple answer, things were so complicated, and this is what bothers me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two questions of a technical nature. When there was a plan of the HVO in place I'm -- I'm saying in such cases in technical terms, maybe that is not your personal forte because it's a technical issue, when the HVO organised an attack or planned an attack in -- did the intelligence service in -- as far as you know, did they have to make a specific reference to the plan that had been prepared about the execution of the plan, and did they have to mention the number of the plan and -- or, rather, you have just said that according to you the information had to be neutral or objective. They didn't -- the intelligence service did not have to comment. They just had to provide raw information to the authorities. So what would be the situation? How did the things develop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is as follows: If there had been any plan for the HVO attack on the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he would first have a report on the strength of the forces, their deployment, a map, the beginning of the attack and the development of the attack. None of that existed. At least I never any of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The soldier who was killed, and obviously it is a murder that triggered everything, was he killed by a sniper? How was he killed? It's mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was killed at the check-point at Makljen. He was simply killed, just like that, without any reason at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the death of the soldier had an impact on the military actions afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the trigger that set fire to the dry grass that existed there already. JUDGE: So it's a flare, when you say Iskra.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
